content: `.glass-panel` is a plain (unlayered) class declared *after* `@tailwind utilities`, so in the compiled stylesheet it comes after every utility of equal specificity (0,1,0) and silently wins. At its ~25 call sites this breaks the intended per-instance styling: `border: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,0.1)` overrides `border-2 border-game-neonCyan` / `border-gray-700/80`, and `box-shadow: 0 8px 32px ...` overrides `shadow-2xl` and the inline `shadow-[0_0_80px_rgba(255,215,0,0.6)]` glows. Wrap the helper rules (`.glass-panel`, `.glass-card`, `.neon-glow-*`) in `@layer components` (emitted before utilities) so call sites can keep overriding them; remember to close the layer after the last helper. Utilities in `@layer components` are also dropped when unused.

`.glass-card` is missing the `-webkit-backdrop-filter` prefix that `.glass-panel` has (needed by Safari < 18), so on those engines it silently degrades to a 60%-alpha panel over arbitrary content, which can hurt readability. Additionally this helper is never referenced anywhere in the codebase (only `.glass-panel` is used) ΓÇö either remove the dead rule or keep it consistent with `.glass-panel` by adding the prefixed property.

None of the `.neon-glow-*` classes are referenced by any component (call sites use Tailwind `shadow-[...]` / `animate-pulse-glow` instead), so they ship dead CSS on every page together with `.glass-card`. Either delete them or move them into `@layer components` so Tailwind emits them only when used. The hardcoded rgba values also duplicate `game.neonCyan` / `game.neonRed` / `game.neonGold` from `tailwind.config.js`, giving two sources of truth for the neon palette.

These two tokens are never referenced anywhere in the project ΓÇö the `body` gradient hardcodes `#171f33` / `#0a0d14` instead, and `#171f33` does not even match either token value. This leaves a dead, drifting source of truth for the background palette (a third one being `colors.game.*` in `tailwind.config.js`). Drive the gradient from these variables, or delete them.

The `background` shorthand resets `background-color` to `transparent`, so the gradient is the only paint on the canvas: if it is ever unsupported, overridden (e.g. by a utility class on `<body>`) or not yet decoded, users get a white/UA-default flash on an otherwise dark theme. Add an explicit solid fallback and use `background-image` explicitly so later rules can override just the image.

Hiding horizontal overflow globally masks genuine layout overflow instead of fixing it: any container wider than the viewport (leaderboard rows, `BoardGrid`, modals) gets silently clipped with no way to scroll to the hidden part, and it makes overflow regressions invisible during development. Because `overflow` on `body` propagates to the viewport it can also change scroll-container/sticky behaviour unexpectedly. Fix the offending container (`min-w-0`, `max-w-full`, `overflow-x-auto` where scrolling is actually wanted) rather than masking it here.

Scrollbar theming is WebKit-only: Firefox and other engines ignore `::-webkit-scrollbar*` and keep a light native scrollbar, and `color-scheme: dark` is never declared anywhere, so UA-rendered scrollbars/form controls stay light against this dark theme. Add `color-scheme: dark` on `:root`, the standard `scrollbar-width`/`scrollbar-color` properties, and style `::-webkit-scrollbar-corner` (otherwise a light square shows where both scrollbars meet). The 6px width is also hard to grab on touch devices ΓÇö 8ΓÇô10px is a safer minimum.

`eslint.ignoreDuringBuilds: true` silently skips all lint enforcement during `next build`. This is especially risky here because `frontend/package.json` defines no `lint` script and the project has no ESLint dependency/config (`eslint-config-next` is absent), so linting is effectively never executed anywhere. Lint regressions (e.g. `react-hooks/exhaustive-deps`, `jsx-a11y`, security-related rules) can therefore reach production unnoticed, and with `ignoreBuildErrors: false` this is the only remaining static quality gate at build time. Recommend either removing this override so the build fails on lint errors, or adding a standalone lint step (`next lint` + `eslint-config-next`, wired into CI) and treating this bypass as a documented, temporary measure.

Unless there is a concrete migration blocker, prefer enabling `strict` (or at least these individual flags) so these classes of bugs are caught at compile time instead of at runtime.

content: `origin: '*'` combined with `credentials: true` is an unsafe and effectively broken CORS policy: browsers reject credentialed responses when `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` is `*`, and if the origin were reflected instead, any third-party site could send authenticated requests to this API (CSRF/data exposure). Restrict allowed origins to an explicit allowlist (ideally from configuration/env).

`bootstrap()` is called without any error handling, so a startup failure (e.g. port already in use, module init error) becomes an unhandled promise rejection with no log and a zero/undefined exit code, which makes container/supervisor restarts and diagnostics unreliable. Chain a `.catch()` that logs the failure and exits with a non-zero code.

`process.env.PORT` is passed to `listen()` without validation and the fallback `3001` is hardcoded. A non-numeric value (e.g. `PORT=abc`) silently produces a confusing runtime failure instead of a clear startup error; the default port should also come from configuration rather than being inlined. Parse and range-check the value before using it.

`durationSeconds` is never validated. Passing `NaN` (or `Infinity`) makes `this.remaining` NaN, so `this.remaining <= 0` is always false and the interval runs forever, ticking `NaN` every second and never releasing resources. Negative values emit negative tick values, and `0` emits `0` on the initial tick but only expires one second later. Validate the input before starting the countdown.

`onTick` is invoked before the expiry check and `the interval callback` reads `this.onTickCallback`/`this.remaining` after the user callback returns. If `onTick` (or code it triggers, e.g. a socket handler) calls `clear()` or `start()`, the following `this.remaining <= 0` check evaluates mutated/re-initialized state, which can fire `onExpire` for a timer that was already cancelled or double-trigger expiry. Capture the callback locally and guard the expiry branch with a generation/token check (or set a flag before invoking callbacks) so a cancelled timer cannot expire.

Deriving `remaining` by decrementing on every interval firing accumulates `setInterval` drift and event-loop stalls, so a "5s/15s" countdown can be noticeably off (the interval is not guaranteed to fire exactly every 1000 ms). Compute the remaining time from a wall-clock deadline (`Date.now()` captured in `start()`, e.g. `Math.ceil((deadline - Date.now()) / 1000)`) and stop when it reaches 0.

`clear()` stops the timers but keeps `onTickCallback`/`onExpireCallback` (and the stale `remaining`) referenced. Since the callbacks close over gateway/game state, this retains that state after the countdown ends and makes a `getRemaining()`/callback invocation on a stopped timer possible. Null the callbacks (and reset state) here ΓÇö take care to capture `onExpireCallback` before calling `clear()` in the expiry branch so the callback still fires.

Dead code: `this.timer` is only ever read/cleared and is never assigned a value anywhere, so the `clearTimeout` branch in `clear()` is unreachable. Either restore the timeout mechanism that was intended to use this field or delete the field and the branch.
Dead code: `this.duration` is assigned in `start()` but never read anywhere in the class, so it carries no information. Remove it or use it (e.g. for progress calculation).

`sessionId` is a bearer credential: `GameService.reconnectPlayer()` (`backend/src/game/game.service.ts:174`) lets any caller take over a player purely by presenting this value. Because the whole `GameRoom`/`Player` object is returned by `getRoom()` and broadcast to *all* sockets (`GameGateway.broadcastRoomState()` -> `room:updated`, plus `room:state` on connect), every client in the room receives other players' `sessionId`s and can impersonate them (and disconnect/kick the real owner via the socket-id remap). Keep the session token server-side only: omit it from the broadcast shape (e.g. return a sanitized DTO from `getRoom()` or strip `sessionId` before emit) and, ideally, rotate it when a reconnect is consumed.

content: This service is a NestJS singleton, so `setCustomGame` overwrites the process-wide `defaultQuestions` and `secretMedia` for every connected user/room. One client submitting a custom game silently replaces the questions and secret answer for all concurrent sessions, and interleaved requests race on the same shared object. content: `GameConfigPayload` bundles the round answer (`secretMedia.keyword`) and `Question.correctIndex` together with player-visible data, and the name ("Payload") suggests it is a network payload. Nothing in the type marks it as host/server-only, so any consumer that serialises it (e.g. over HTTP/socket) leaks the secret answer to players. Add an explicit JSDoc contract (server/host-only, never broadcast) and/or split a sanitised public DTO without `keyword`/`correctIndex`.

`QuestionBank` re-declares `secretMedia`/`questions`, which are already declared on `GameConfigPayload` in the same file, so the two shapes can drift. (It is also exported but never referenced anywhere, i.e. effectively dead code.) Make it extend `GameConfigPayload` instead of duplicating the fields.

`Question` is owned by the game module while question data/configuration is owned by this module (questions -> game dependency), and `GameConfigPayload` is not imported by any consumer ΓÇö the equivalent shape is re-declared inline elsewhere (e.g. `resetRoomWithConfig` in game.service and the Studio modal), so the contract has multiple sources of truth and can silently drift. Keep a single source of truth by importing these types from here, or extract the shared domain types into a neutral module. (The current direction is acyclic ΓÇö game does not import questions ΓÇö so this is a consolidation concern, not a circular-import bug.)

`this.ctx.resume()` returns a promise that is neither awaited nor caught. If it rejects (autoplay policy without a user gesture, or a context that was closed), the rejection is unhandled and `getAudioContext()` still hands back a context whose state is `'suspended'`, so every scheduled note is silently dropped or queued and callers have no idea playback failed. Handle the rejection explicitly (the calling play methods are synchronous, so at least swallow/log it instead of leaving an unhandled rejection).

`(window as any)` violates the project's no-`any` rule and erases the type of the vendor-prefixed constructor. Type the prefixed property explicitly (with a short comment explaining why the cast is needed) instead of falling back to `any`.

`new AudioCtx()` can throw (browser context limit reached, audio disabled in the environment). Because the public play methods are called directly from UI event handlers, an uncaught exception here would propagate into the React handler and break the interaction. Wrap construction in a try/catch and degrade gracefully to no sound.

The oscillator/gain creation, connection, start/stop and volume/duration values are duplicated in all four play methods, with the magic numbers (frequencies, gains, durations) inlined per method. This makes the sounds drift apart easily. Consider extracting a private helper (e.g. `playTone(ctx, { type, frequency, startAt, duration, volume })`) and hoisting the tone/volume constants so each sound is just a declarative note list.

Stopped oscillators/gain nodes are left connected to `ctx.destination`; nothing disconnects them when playback finishes, so repeated correct-answer triggers keep finished nodes referenced by the audio graph until GC decides to clean them up. Disconnect in the `onended` handler to release the nodes deterministically.

`socket: socketRef.current` is evaluated at render time, so the first render returns `null` and later renders keep returning the socket captured in that render. Because mutating a ref never triggers a re-render, consumers that do `const { socket } = useSocket(...)` and then `socket.on(...)` can throw on mount or silently attach listeners to a socket that the effect has already replaced. Return the ref itself (consumers read `socketRef.current` at call time), or mirror the instance into state so re-renders deliver the live socket. Note that none of the current call sites actually use this field, so removing it is also an option.

Alert auto-dismiss timers are fire-and-forget: the handles are never stored or cleared. Consequences: (1) any older timeout will clear a newer alert (e.g. a `buzzer:rejected` alert wiped by an earlier `session:invalid` timer), (2) timers are not cleared on unmount, so they call `setAlertMessage` after the component is gone (stale-state/leak warning), and (3) the exact same block is duplicated for every alert source. Extract a single helper backed by a ref-held timeout that clears the previous timer, and clear it in the effect cleanup.

The socket is created and the whole listener set is torn down whenever `role` or `initialName` changes. Any change to `initialName` (e.g. the caller re-renders with an edited/default name) disconnects a live game and re-emits join/reconnect, losing session continuity; the tests also depend on this behavior. Additionally, cleanup only disconnects the socket and leaves `room`, `me`, `isHostAuthenticated`, `timerRemaining`/`timerType` populated, so state from the previous room/session is shown against a brand-new socket. Read the name through a ref (or rely on `joinGame`) and keep the effect keyed only on `role`, and reset per-socket state in the cleanup.

`connect` also fires after a socket.io reconnection, and a reconnected socket gets a **new** `id`. Server-side host authorization is stored per socket id (`authenticatedHostSockets` keyed by `client.id` in `game.service.ts`), so after any network blip the client keeps `isHostAuthenticated === true` while the server rejects every host action with an 'Unauthorized' error. Reset (and ideally re-prompt for the PIN) on `connect`, or re-emit `host:authenticate` with a stored PIN.

`config: any` violates the project rule against `any` and removes all type/validation safety on data that is forwarded straight to `host:create_custom_game`. Define a `CustomGameConfig` interface (questions/time limit/total rounds, mirroring what the backend `resetRoomWithConfig` consumes) and reuse it here instead.

`reconnectionAttempts: 10` is configured but no `connect_error` (or `reconnect_failed`) listener is registered, and the hook doesn't listen for `connect_error` to set `isConnected`/surface an error. Once the attempts are exhausted the UI stays silently offline: `isConnected` is false but the user gets no actionable message. Add a `connect_error` handler that sets `isConnected` and shows a user-friendly alert (and consider also surfacing a retry hint).

`room:state` and `room:updated` are handled by byte-for-byte identical callbacks (same for `player:joined` and `player:reconnected`). Extract a single `applyRoomUpdate(updatedRoom)` / `applyPlayerSession(player)` function and register it under both event names ΓÇö this also gives one place to reset `timerRemaining`/`timerType` when a room update arrives.

The Spacebar guard only excludes `INPUT`, and `e.repeat` is never checked. content: The modal returns `null` when closed but stays mounted, so all `useState` initializers run only once: edits made in a previous session persist across close/reopen, and any later change to the `initialConfig` prop is silently ignored (stale data). Reset/sync the editable state when the modal is (re)opened, e.g. via a `useEffect` keyed on `isOpen`/`initialConfig`, or have the parent mount it only while open (`{isOpen && <GameStudioModal ... />}` / a `key`).

content: Apply-time validation only rejects empty text/options. Option count (must be 4), `correctIndex` bounds, `id` presence and `timeLimit` validity are never checked, so a malformed imported/edited deck can be applied to the whole room and produce unplayable cards/questions. Extend the guard to check option array length, `Number.isInteger(correctIndex) && correctIndex >= 0 && correctIndex < options.length`, and sanitize `timeLimit`.
suggestion_code:
const isAllValid = questions.every(
      (q) =>
        typeof q.text === 'string' &&
        q.text.trim() &&
        Array.isArray(q.options) &&
        q.options.length === 4 &&
        q.options.every((o) => typeof o === 'string' && o.trim()) &&
        Number.isInteger(q.correctIndex) &&
        q.correctIndex >= 0 &&
        q.correctIndex < q.options.length,
    );

content: The object URL is revoked synchronously right after `link.click()`; in some browsers the download has not started yet, so the blob may already be invalidated and the export fails. Revoke it asynchronously (e.g. `setTimeout(() => URL.revokeObjectURL(url), 0)`), and consider appending/removing the anchor for maximum browser compatibility.

content: This icon selection is a 3ΓÇô4 level nested ternary, which is explicitly disallowed by the project rules and hard to read/maintain (it also duplicates the state branches already computed for `colorStyle`). Pre-compute the icon with a flat if/else chain (or a small `renderIcon()` helper) before the `return` and render `{icon}` in the JSX.

The steal-mode award of `+150 ─æiß╗âm` is a business value hardcoded in the UI layer; if the scoring config changes this text silently becomes wrong. Pass the amount in via props (or read it from the shared game config). The cooldown copy `(1 l╞░ß╗út)` above has the same problem ΓÇö the turn count should come from the game settings rather than being duplicated here.

`handleClick` only guards on the `isDisabled` prop, which is derived from parent state. Rapid repeated taps before the parent re-renders (or on slow devices) can invoke `onBuzz()` more than once, potentially submitting duplicate buzzes. Add a local latch (e.g. a `useRef` set on the first buzz and reset when the buzzer/steal state changes) and/or make the parent handler idempotent for a given buzz window.

These are static inline styles: `WebkitTapHighlightColor` and the fixed `animationDuration: '8s'` on the Snowflake icon never change at runtime. The project rules reserve the `style` attribute for dynamic values only ΓÇö move both to CSS/Tailwind classes (e.g. a utility class for the slow spin), keeping inline styles out of the (re)render path.

`isFrozen` is typed as a number (a turn count, used as `isFrozen > 0`) but the `is` prefix conventionally indicates a boolean, which is misleading at call sites. Rename it to something like `frozenTurns` / `frozenCount`.

The studio config is effectively never applied. `GameStudioModal` is mounted here unconditionally on the first render, when `room` is still `null` (state arrives later via `room:state`), and the modal derives its state from `initialConfig` only through `useState` initializers (`useState(initialConfig?.secretMedia?.keyword || 'Vß╗ïnh Hß║í Long')` etc.). Because the modal instance is never remounted, later changes to this prop are ignored, so opening Game Studio during an active match shows the hardcoded dummy deck instead of the live keyword/questions. The object is also recreated on every render (new reference each `room` update), which prevents any prop-based memo/sync from working. Consider mounting the modal only while open (e.g. `{isStudioOpen && <GameStudioModal ... />}`) or keying/syncing the modal from this config.

content: The requestAnimationFrame loop is never cancelled ΓÇö the effect returns no cleanup, so after unmount the loop keeps emitting confetti until the 5s window elapses, and React StrictMode's double-invocation starts two overlapping loops (doubled particle density, duplicated work). Track the RAF id (declare `let rafId: number | undefined;` before `frame` and assign it inside) and cancel it in the effect cleanup; also reset the canvas with `confetti.reset()` so ongoing particles stop on unmount. Consider exposing the 5s duration as a prop/constant instead of an inline magic number.

`winnerName` has a fallback, but `secretImageUrl`/`secretKeyword` do not. The parent (`screen/page.tsx`) passes `room?.secretImageUrl || ''`, so when the game ends without a stored image this renders a blank/broken image frame (with an empty `alt`) and gives the user no feedback. Guard against an empty URL and add an `onError` fallback so a failed load also shows a placeholder instead of the broken-image icon.

content: `NEXT_PUBLIC_BACKEND_URL` is passed as a build arg, and Next.js inlines `NEXT_PUBLIC_*` variables into the client bundle at build time. The default `http://localhost:3001` therefore gets baked into the shipped image; any browser not running on the Docker host will try to reach its own localhost and all API/socket calls will fail. It also means changing the value requires a full image rebuild rather than a restart. Prefer serving the API through the same origin (reverse proxy / relative URL), or read the backend URL at runtime instead of relying on a build-time public variable.
